S01.label: Understanding friendship levels
S01.definition: Distinguish acquaintances, potential friends, friends, and best friends, with realistic expectations.

S02.label: Recognizing healthy friendships
S02.definition: Recognize trust, safety, respect, reciprocity, listening, and support in relationships.

S03.label: Recognizing bullying
S03.definition: Distinguish bullying from accidents and ordinary conflict using purpose, pattern, and power.

S04.label: Responding safely to bullying
S04.definition: Use practiced responses, supportive friends, and trusted adults when targeted or witnessing bullying.

S05.label: Naming and understanding feelings
S05.definition: Identify emotions, their intensity, and mixed feelings, and connect them to situations.

S06.label: Understanding others' feelings
S06.definition: Notice emotional cues and consider another person's feelings and perspective.

S07.label: Noticing body signals
S07.definition: Recognize physical signs of emotions or stress, such as tension or a racing heart.

S08.label: Calming intense feelings
S08.definition: Use breathing, pauses, grounding activities, or other coping strategies when emotions become intense.

S09.label: Replacing unhelpful thoughts
S09.definition: Identify extreme or inaccurate thoughts and replace them with realistic, balanced alternatives.

S10.label: Adapting to changed plans
S10.definition: Adjust expectations and responses when situations change or plans do not work out.

S11.label: Making backup plans
S11.definition: Anticipate obstacles and use if-then planning or alternative actions to handle them.

S12.label: Understanding figurative language
S12.definition: Recognize idioms, exaggerations, and expressions whose meaning differs from their literal words.

S13.label: Interpreting communication in context
S13.definition: Use the situation, tone, facial expressions, and other cues to understand meaning and timing.

S14.label: Choosing kind and honest words
S14.definition: Consider the impact of words and communicate with care and honesty.

S15.label: Taking turns in conversation
S15.definition: Listen, share speaking time, and recognize when another person wants a turn.

S16.label: Asking questions that build connection
S16.definition: Ask relevant follow-up and open-ended questions that keep a conversation going.

S17.label: Joining respectfully
S17.definition: Check permission before entering another person's activity or space.

S18.label: Managing the urge to interrupt
S18.definition: Notice triggers and use waiting, signaling, or idea-parking strategies before speaking.

S19.label: Taking responsibility
S19.definition: Own one's actions and contribution to a problem instead of denying it or blaming others.

S20.label: Apologizing and repairing harm
S20.definition: Acknowledge what happened, take responsibility, and act to repair a hurt or mistake.

S21.label: Learning from mistakes
S21.definition: Treat mistakes as learning opportunities, reflect, and persist with a growth mindset.

S22.label: Practicing self-kindness
S22.definition: Respond to mistakes with compassion and challenge unfair self-blame without avoiding responsibility.

S23.label: Managing performance stress
S23.definition: Recognize helpful versus overwhelming stress before, during, and after tests, presentations, games, or performances.

S24.label: Acting with compassion
S24.definition: Choose helpful, kind actions in response to others' needs without expecting something in return.

S25.label: Resolving conflict fairly
S25.definition: Calm down, share needs, listen, brainstorm, and find a solution that respects both people.

questions.text: When your child thinks about their friendships, which sounds most like them?

answers.text: They understand how close different friendships are and can recognize when someone treats them with care.
They sometimes expect a new or casual friend to act like a very close friend.
They find it hard to tell whether a friendship is respectful and supportive.
Both of those things can be difficult for them.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: When someone repeatedly treats your child or another child unkindly, which sounds most like them?

answers.text: They can recognize when it may be bullying and know how to get support from a trusted adult.
They are unsure whether it is bullying or an ordinary disagreement.
They recognize that something is wrong but are unsure what to do or who to ask for help.
They need help both understanding what is happening and knowing how to respond.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: When someone around your child is upset or needs help, which sounds most like them?

answers.text: They usually notice and can think of a kind way to help when they are able to.
They often need help noticing or understanding how the other person feels.
They notice how the person feels but need help thinking of a kind action they could take.
They need help both understanding the person's feelings and choosing how to help.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: During an everyday disagreement with a friend or sibling, which sounds most like your child?

answers.text: They can work toward a fair solution and try to repair any hurt they caused.
They find it hard to listen to both sides and work toward a fair solution.
They can work out the disagreement but need help apologizing or repairing hurt they caused.
They need help both finding a fair solution and repairing any hurt they caused.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: When your child starts to feel upset, which sounds most like them?

answers.text: They can usually name the feeling and notice clues in their body.
They notice something feels different in their body but find it hard to name the feeling.
They can name the feeling but often miss early body clues, such as tension or a racing heart.
They need help both naming the feeling and noticing body clues.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: When feelings get big, which sounds most like your child?

answers.text: They have ways to settle their feelings and can keep the situation in perspective.
They need help finding a way to settle their feelings.
Thoughts such as 'Everything is ruined' make the feelings harder to handle.
They need help both settling their feelings and finding a more balanced way to think about what happened.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: When a plan changes or something does not work out, which sounds most like your child?

answers.text: They can adjust to the change and think of something else to do.
They can think of another option but find it hard to accept the change.
They can accept the change but need help thinking of another option.
They need help both adjusting to the change and making a new plan.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: When your child hears an expression or a message that is not straightforward, which sounds most like them?

answers.text: They can usually work out what is meant from the words and the situation.
They take expressions such as 'hold your horses' literally and need help understanding them.
They understand familiar expressions but can miss meaning shown by the situation or tone of voice.
They need help both understanding expressions and using clues from the situation.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: When your child has a conversation, which sounds most like them?

answers.text: They give the other person a turn and ask questions about what that person shares.
They often keep talking without giving the other person much chance to speak.
They take turns but need help asking questions that keep the conversation going.
They need help both sharing speaking time and asking questions.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: When your child speaks to someone, which sounds most like them?

answers.text: They usually notice how the person feels and choose words that show care.
They notice how the person feels, but their words can sound hurtful or sharper than they intended.
They try to speak kindly but need help understanding how the other person feels.
They need help both understanding the person's feelings and choosing kind words.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: After your child does something that causes a problem, which sounds most like them?

answers.text: They can acknowledge their part and take a step to put things right.
They often blame someone else or deny what happened.
They acknowledge their part but need help apologizing or putting things right.
They need help both acknowledging their part and putting things right.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: When your child wants to speak or join an activity, which sounds most like them?

answers.text: They can wait for a turn and check before joining someone else's activity.
They usually check before joining an activity but find it hard to wait before speaking.
They can wait before speaking but sometimes join someone else's activity without checking.
They need help both waiting before speaking and checking before joining.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: Around a test, presentation, game, or performance, where does your child most often need support?

answers.text: Their nerves are manageable and they can take part.
Before it starts: worry makes starting or taking part difficult.
While it is happening: nerves or mistakes make it hard to keep going.
Afterward: they replay what went wrong and find it hard to feel good about their effort.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: When your child is disappointed in themselves, which sounds most like them?

answers.text: They can treat themselves kindly and think fairly about what happened.
They know mistakes are normal but still find it hard to be kind to themselves.
They get stuck on thoughts such as 'I always get everything wrong,' even when that is not true.
They need help both being kind to themselves and finding a fairer way to think about what happened.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

questions.text: After something is difficult or goes wrong, which sounds most like your child?

answers.text: They can learn from what happened and try again.
They often see a mistake as proof that they are not good at something.
They avoid another try because they are afraid of getting it wrong.
They want to try again but need help figuring out what to learn or change.
I'm not sure, or I have not seen this situation.

modules.title: Levels of Friendship
modules.basis: Friendship stages, social indicators, and friends versus best friends.

modules.title: Dealing with Bullying
modules.basis: Identification and safe responses are central. Emotional awareness, calming, and reframing support those responses.

modules.title: Dealing with Unexpected Change
modules.basis: Flexibility and practical/emotional if-then planning are central. Coping and helpful thoughts support adaptation.

modules.title: Recognizing & Identifying Feelings
modules.basis: Naming feelings, noticing body/thought clues, and managing feelings form the three concepts. Friendly self-talk supports coping.

modules.title: Managing Overreactions
modules.basis: Emotion identification, reframing, and emotional adaptability are explicit concepts. Calming is directly practiced through a coping toolbox.

modules.title: Literal & Figurative Language
modules.basis: Literal/figurative meaning, context clues, and everyday expressions.

modules.title: Speaking Kindly and Honestly
modules.basis: Word impact, reading others' feelings, and repairing mistakes are central. Context and ownership support those skills.

modules.title: Conversation Skills - Asking Questions
modules.basis: Balanced conversation, question-asking, and question types are central. Perspective and cues support the exchange.

modules.title: Taking Responsibility & Not Blaming Others
modules.basis: Ownership is the central outcome. Naming hard feelings, pausing, apologizing, and learning help children choose it.

modules.title: Learning From Mistakes
modules.basis: Normalizing mistakes and growth mindset are central. Recognizing shame/fear, reframing, honesty, and encouragement support learning.

modules.title: Waiting Your Turn
modules.basis: Interrupting/intruding, triggers, waiting, and permission/signaling strategies are central. Calming and considering others support them.

modules.title: Overcoming Performance Stress
modules.basis: Before/during/after performance stress is the central context. Body awareness, coping, reframing, adaptability, reflection, and kindness support it.

modules.title: Being Kind to Yourself
modules.basis: Self-talk/reframing, challenging self-blame, and self-kindness are central. Mistake normalization reinforces them.

modules.title: Being Considerate
modules.basis: Empathy, compassion, and fair conflict resolution are central. Calming and repair support resolving disagreements.
